title: Identifiers, keywords, literals
hook: C# is case-sensitive. Keywords are reserved. Literals are typed values in source — and since C# 11, raw string literals are the honest way to paste JSON or CSV headers without escape soup.

sections.heading: Names, reserved words, comments
sections.prose: Identifiers start with a letter or underscore (Unicode letters allowed). `@event` lets you use a keyword as a name — you see it in wrappers around JS-ish APIs. Keywords (`if`, `class`, `int`, `await`) cannot be reused without `@`. Contextual keywords (`from`, `var`, `yield`) are reserved only in specific grammars. Comments are `//`, `/* */`, and XML `///` for docs. Unlike JS, there is no automatic semicolon insertion: omit `;` and you get a compile error, not a mystery ASI bug.

snippets.label: Raw string literal vs escaped JSON
snippets.explanation: Raw strings start with at least three quotes. Interpolation uses `$"""` and `{{` for braces. Prefer them for EventBridge sample JSON in tests.

sections.heading: Literal kinds you will actually type
sections.prose: `199` is int, `199L` long, `0xFF` hex, `0b1010` binary, `1.5` double, `1.5m` decimal (money/grades later), `'A'` char, `"hi"` string, `"""..."""` raw string, `$"count={n}"` interpolated, `true`/`false`/`null`. Digit separators `1_000` are legal. Verbatim `"C:\temp"` still exists; raw strings usually read better.

interviewTakeaways: C# does not have ASI; statements end with semicolons or are structured (`if`/`for`).
Raw string literals (C# 11) are the default answer for multi-line JSON/CSV in source.
`@` escapes keywords; it does not create a different CLR name besides the identifier.
commonPitfalls: Using `1.5` (double) for money literals — you wanted `1.5m`.
Interpolating JSON with `$"{ ... }"` and fighting braces; use `$"""` raw interpolation.
Treating `var` as a keyword that makes the variable dynamic — it is inferred static type.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS ASI and template strings (`backticks`) are the closest analog to C# semicolons and `$"""` raw interpolated strings, but C# interpolation is typed.
